intro: Long ago, a race at Olympia had one result: the winner's name. Nobody could say how fast anyone ran. Swimmers raced in the sea, and tennis was played in stone halls with walls. Every place did things its own way.

Over time, people measured these places and wrote the measurements down. A track became 400 meters around. An Olympic pool became 50 meters long. A tennis court became a rectangle 78 feet long. Clubs, federations and the IHSA in Illinois kept the rules and the records.

In this unit you will meet the people who did that work, and the people who were shut out and then let in. You will be able to explain how a lap, a lane and a painted line let a runner, a swimmer or a player in one town compare with someone far away.
bigQuestion: How did measured tracks, pools and courts let people in different places compete fairly?

title: Time, Water, a Line

chapters.title: A Clock on a Track
chapters.bigQuestion: How did people turn a footrace into a time that anyone, anywhere, could check?

story.title: Eight Lanes, Eight Times
story.kicker: A hand drops at the start, and far away, eight clocks begin to count.
paragraphs: It is a cool spring evening at a school track in Illinois. Eight runners wait at their marks in eight painted lanes. Parents sit on metal bleachers. A fourth grader named Luis sits with his grandfather, who ran on this same track in 1970.
The starter lifts a pistol. Next to him, a helper raises one arm high. When the pistol cracks, the arm drops. At the finish line, a row of timers sees the arm fall and presses their watches.

"When I ran here, the track was black cinders," Grandpa says. "It was made from burned coal. Our times were written by hand on a clipboard." Luis looks at the red rubber under the runners' feet and at the big glowing clock by the finish.

The race ends in seconds. Eight names go up on the board, each with a number beside it. "Now a girl in Rockford can see that time and compare it to hers," Grandpa says. "That is what the clock gives us."
Luis thinks about the old Greek runners his class read about. They had no clocks at all. Only the winner's name was kept. He wonders how people learned to catch something as fast as a second.
story.think: Why might it matter that a time can travel to another town, but a cheer cannot?

lessons.title: The Stadion at Olympia
lessons.mainIdea: The oldest famous footrace was the stadion, a straight dash down a dirt track at Olympia in Greece.
reading: Olympia is a holy place in southern Greece. The ancient Greeks held the Olympic Games there. Greek writers later counted the first Games from 776 BCE. Historians use that date as a tradition, not a proven fact.

The first event on the list was one footrace. It was called the *stadion*. Runners dashed straight down a dirt track, about 192 meters long. There was no curve and no oval. Our word "stadium" comes from this race.

Stone slabs still lie across both ends of the track at Olympia. Each slab has grooves cut into it. This was the *starting line*, made to last. The stone lines seen today were set in place more than 2,000 years ago, and visitors can still stand on them.

words.d: a holy place in southern Greece where the ancient Olympic Games were held
an ancient Greek footrace one track length long; also the name of that length
the marked place where every runner begins a race

look.title: A track with no curve
look.text: Picture a long, flat strip of packed dirt between grassy banks. There are no seats, only slopes where people stood or sat. At each end lies a row of stone slabs with grooves. This is the stadium at Olympia, in Greece.
look.prompt: What clues tell you this place was built for a race?

lessons.title: Winners, Not Times
lessons.mainIdea: Ancient Greeks kept lists of winners' names, but no one could measure how fast a runner ran.
reading: The ancient Greeks had sundials and water clocks. Neither could split a moment into seconds. So a race had only one result: who crossed first. Second place was not recorded at the Olympic Games.
Around 400 BCE, a writer named Hippias of Elis made a *victor list*. It named Olympic winners going back to the first Games. The first name on it was Koroibos of Elis, a stadion winner.

Later Greek writers doubted parts of the list. Plutarch, writing around 100 CE, said Hippias had no strong proof for the oldest names. So historians treat the early names as *tradition*, and the later names as better records.

words.d: a written list of the winners of a contest, year by year
a story or custom handed down over time, which may not be fully proven

look.prompt: Why would Plutarch doubt the oldest names on the list?

check.why: The Greeks could not measure seconds. They kept the winner's name.

check.why: Hippias of Elis made the victor list around 400 BCE.

check.q: Why do historians call the earliest names a tradition?
choices: Even ancient writers like Plutarch doubted them.
They were written by the runners.
check.why: Plutarch said Hippias had no strong proof for the oldest names.

lessons.title: Who Could Run at Olympia
lessons.mainIdea: Only free Greek men and boys could compete at the ancient Olympics; girls had a separate footrace at Olympia.
reading: The ancient Olympic Games had strict rules about who could enter. Athletes had to be free men or boys who spoke Greek. Enslaved people could not compete. Married women were barred even from watching the Games.

Girls had their own festival at Olympia, called the *Heraia*. It honored the goddess Hera. Unmarried girls ran a footrace there, on a course about one-sixth shorter than the men's. The Greek writer Pausanias described it around 170 CE.
The Olympic Games ran for more than a thousand years. They ended after Christian Roman emperors banned old festivals. Historians often give 393 CE as the end, but they are not sure of the exact year.

words.d: a festival at Olympia for the goddess Hera, with a footrace for girls
to take part in a contest against others

look.title: Four dates from Olympia
look.text: 776 BCE: the traditional date of the first Games. About 400 BCE: Hippias of Elis writes his victor list. About 170 CE: Pausanias describes the girls' race at the Heraia. 393 CE: the date most often given for the end of the Games.

check.why: The rules allowed only free men and boys who spoke Greek.

check.q: Who described the Heraia around 170 CE?
check.why: The Greek writer Pausanias described the girls' race at Olympia.

lessons.title: Clubs Write the Rules
lessons.mainIdea: In England, running clubs of the 1860s and 1880s wrote shared rules, and a world body followed in 1912.
reading: In the 1800s, English schools and colleges held footraces. Each place had its own rules. In 1866, men in London formed the Amateur Athletic Club. An *amateur* is someone who competes without being paid.

The club's early rule had a hard edge. It shut out any "mechanic, artisan or labourer." That meant people who worked with their hands could not enter. In 1880, a new group called the Amateur Athletic Association formed at Oxford. It dropped that rule.

Countries soon needed one set of rules for all. In 1912, right after the Olympic Games in Stockholm, Sweden, leaders formed the International Amateur Athletic Federation. In 2019 it took a new name: *World Athletics*.

words.d: someone who takes part in a sport without being paid
the world body for track and field, founded in 1912 and renamed in 2019

lessons.title: Cinders, Then Rubber
lessons.mainIdea: Tracks changed from dirt and cinders to rubber-like surfaces, which first appeared at the Olympics in 1968.
reading: For many years, running tracks were made of *cinders*. Cinders are the gritty bits left after coal burns. Workers packed them into a flat path. Cinders were cheap, because cities and factories burned a lot of coal.
Cinder tracks had problems. Rain turned them to mud. Dry weather made them dusty. A track could be fast one day and slow the next. That made it hard to compare times from different days.

In the 1960s, companies made tracks from rubber-like plastic. These are called *synthetic* tracks. The 1968 Olympic Games in Mexico City were the first Olympics run on one. Today most school tracks in Illinois are synthetic.

words.d: gritty bits left after coal burns, once packed down to make tracks
made by people from chemicals, like a rubber-like plastic track

look.title: Two tracks, same race
look.text: On Monday it rains, and a cinder track turns soft and muddy. On Friday the sun shines, and the same track is hard and dry. The same runner races both days. On a synthetic track, rain drains away and the surface stays the same.
look.prompt: Why might a coach trust the Friday time more than the Monday time on cinders?

check.why: Rain made cinders muddy and sun made them dusty, so conditions changed.

check.q: Which Olympics were first run on a synthetic track?
check.why: The 1968 Games in Mexico City were the first Olympics on a synthetic track.

lessons.title: Why Lane Starts Look Uneven
lessons.mainIdea: A standard track is 400 meters around the inside lane, and outer lanes start farther ahead so every runner goes the same distance.
reading: Most outdoor tracks today are ovals. World Athletics sets the length at 400 meters, measured in the inside *lane*. Each lane is 1.22 meters wide. Many tracks have eight lanes.

An outer lane curves around a bigger circle. If all runners started on one line, the outside runner would go farther. So on curved races, each outer lane starts a little farther ahead. This is called a *stagger*. It keeps the distance equal.
Older American tracks were measured in yards. One lap was 440 yards. That equals about 402 meters, a bit longer than 400. So a time on a yard track and a meter track cannot be matched exactly.

words.d: a marked strip on a track where one runner stays
starting marks set farther ahead in outer lanes so every runner covers the same distance

check.why: An outer lane curves around a bigger circle, so the stagger evens out the distance.

lessons.title: A Watch That Stops
lessons.mainIdea: Stopwatches let race officials write down times, first by hand and in fifths of a second.
reading: In the 1800s, watchmakers built pocket watches that could start and stop on command. These became the *stopwatch*. Now a race could have a number, not just a winner.

Early watches split each second into five parts. So old times look like "10 and 4/5 seconds." People held the watches, so each *timer* pressed a little early or late. Meets often used three timers and kept the middle time.
At the first modern Olympics, in Athens in 1896, Thomas Burke of the United States won the 100 meters. His time was written as 12 seconds. It was timed by hand.

words.d: a watch that can be started and stopped to measure how long something takes
the official who runs a watch and records a race time

look.title: Three watches, one race
look.text: Three timers stand at a finish line in 1920. All three press their watches when the winner crosses. One reads 11 seconds. One reads 11 and 1/5. One reads 11 and 2/5. The meet writes down the middle time.
look.prompt: Why might a meet use three timers instead of one?

check.why: A stopwatch let officials record how long the race took.

check.why: Timers were people, so each one pressed at a slightly different moment.

check.q: Who won the 100 meters at Athens in 1896?
check.why: Thomas Burke of the United States won in 12 seconds, timed by hand.

lessons.title: Cameras at the Finish
lessons.mainIdea: Finish-line cameras and electric clocks replaced hand timing, and since 1977 world records in short races need them.
reading: Sometimes two runners reach the line at almost the same moment. The eye cannot split them. A *photo finish* is a picture taken right at the finish line. It shows who got there first.

At the 1932 Olympics in Los Angeles, judges used a finish-line camera to help decide close races. Over the next decades, cameras and electric clocks got better. They could start with the starting gun and stop at the line.

Electric timing counts in hundredths of a second. Starting in 1977, world records in races up to 400 meters had to be timed electrically. This is called *fully automatic timing*. Hand times no longer counted for those records.

words.d: a picture taken at the finish line to show the exact order of runners
electric timing that starts with the gun and stops at the line, with no person pressing a button

choices: a picture at the finish line that shows the order
check.why: A photo finish is taken at the line to show who arrived first.

check.q: Where did judges use a finish camera at the 1932 Olympics?
check.why: The 1932 Olympics were in Los Angeles.

lessons.title: State Champions Before the IHSA
lessons.mainIdea: IHSA records list boys track champions from 1893, seven years before the association itself began in 1900.
reading: The *IHSA* is the Illinois High School Association. It runs state tournaments for high schools across Illinois. The association was founded in 1900, four years after the first modern Olympics in Athens.

Yet the IHSA's records list boys track and field champions from 1893. That is seven years before the association existed. Illinois schools were already racing each other for a state title. The IHSA kept those early winners in its *record book*.
Track is one of the oldest state series in Illinois. Boys tennis followed, with a first champion in 1912. Many other sports came much later. Timed races made track easy to compare, school to school.

lessons.title: Betty Robinson of Riverdale
lessons.mainIdea: Women first ran track at the Olympics in 1928, and Betty Robinson of Riverdale, Illinois, won the first women's 100 meters.
reading: For decades, Olympic track was for men only. Women's track and field events were added at the 1928 Games in Amsterdam. Some leaders had argued against it. They said women should not race.
Betty Robinson grew up in Riverdale, Illinois, just south of Chicago. In 1928, at age 16, she won the Olympic 100 meters. She was the first woman ever to win an Olympic gold medal in track.
In 1931, Robinson was badly hurt in a plane crash. She could not walk for months. She worked her way back. At the 1936 Games in Berlin, she won a second gold medal in the women's *relay*.

lessons.title: The Paralympic Games
lessons.mainIdea: Games for athletes with disabilities began in England in 1948 and became the first Paralympic Games in Rome in 1960.
reading: Dr. Ludwig Guttmann was a doctor at Stoke Mandeville Hospital in England. He cared for people with spinal injuries, many of them soldiers from World War II. He believed sport helped his patients build strength and hope.

On July 29, 1948, the same day the London Olympics opened, Guttmann held a contest at the hospital. Sixteen wheelchair athletes took part in archery. The event became the Stoke Mandeville Games, held again each year.

In 1960, the games went to Rome, right after the Olympics there. About 400 athletes from 23 countries came. These are now counted as the first *Paralympic Games*. Today, *wheelchair racing* is one of the fastest events on the Paralympic track.

words.d: the world games for athletes with disabilities, first held in Rome in 1960

chapters.title: Pool Length and a Tennis Line
chapters.bigQuestion: How did a stretch of water and a patch of grass become measured places with shared rules?

story.title: A Rope Across the Water
story.kicker: A rope floats across a pool, and a length of water becomes a lane.
paragraphs: Early on a Saturday, Ms. Okafor unlocks the school pool. The water is flat and still. Her helper, a fifth grader named Rosa, carries a coil of rope strung with bright plastic floats.

Together they hook one end of the rope to the wall and float it across the water. Then another, and another. Soon the open water has become eight long lanes, side by side. Each one is exactly 25 yards from wall to wall.

"Why does the length have to be exact?" Rosa asks. Ms. Okafor points at a board on the wall. It lists the school's best times, each with a name and a year. "If this pool were a foot short, every time on that board would be wrong," she says.
Outside the window, a man is painting white lines on the tennis courts. He uses a string and a measuring tape. Rosa watches him check each corner twice.
"He is doing the same thing we are," Ms. Okafor says. "A pool and a court are both drawings. People in England and Greece and Illinois agreed to draw them the same way."
story.think: Why would people in different countries agree to draw a pool or a court the same way?

lessons.title: The Great Bath
lessons.mainIdea: One of the oldest built pools is the Great Bath at Mohenjo-daro, made of brick about 4,500 years ago.
reading: Mohenjo-daro was a large city in the Indus River valley, in what is now Pakistan. People built it around 2500 BCE. Its streets, wells and drains were laid out with care.

In the middle of the city sits the *Great Bath*. It is a sunken tank about 12 meters long and 7 meters wide. Steps lead down at each end. Builders sealed the bricks with a layer of tar so the water would not leak out.

The Great Bath was not built for races. Many scholars think people used it for washing in special ceremonies. It shows how old the idea of a *tank* is: water held in a shape that people planned and measured.

words.d: a large brick pool at Mohenjo-daro, built around 2500 BCE
a large built container that holds water

look.title: Steps into water
look.text: Picture a long rectangle sunk into the ground, lined with tight red bricks. Wide steps go down at both ends. Around it is a walkway with small rooms. The city of Mohenjo-daro spreads out on every side.
look.prompt: What tells you the builders planned this pool carefully?

check.q: Where is the Great Bath?
check.why: The Great Bath is in the old city of Mohenjo-daro in the Indus valley.

check.q: How did builders keep water from leaking out of the Great Bath?
choices: They sealed the bricks with tar.
check.why: A layer of tar sealed the bricks.

check.q: What do many scholars think the Great Bath was used for?
check.why: It was not built for races. Many scholars link it to ceremonies.

lessons.title: Swimming the Channel
lessons.mainIdea: Long swims in open water, like Matthew Webb's English Channel crossing in 1875, made swimming famous before most towns had pools.
reading: The English Channel is the stretch of sea between England and France. At its narrowest, it is about 21 miles across. The water is cold, and the tides push swimmers sideways.

On August 24 and 25, 1875, Captain Matthew Webb swam from Dover, England, to Calais, France. He took almost 22 hours. He was the first person known to cross without a boat or float to hold. Newspapers everywhere reported it.

In 1926, Gertrude Ederle of New York became the first woman to swim the Channel. She did it in about 14 and a half hours. That beat every man who had crossed before her. A huge *parade* welcomed her home in New York City.

words.d: the stretch of sea between England and France
a lake, river or sea, not a built pool
a public march through the streets to celebrate someone

look.text: It is August 1875 on the beach at Dover. A man covered in porpoise grease walks into the gray sea. A small boat with his helpers follows him. France is more than 20 miles away, and the tide will carry him far off a straight line.
look.prompt: Why would a swim across the sea make headlines in 1875, when few towns had pools?

check.why: Webb swam from Dover to Calais in 1875.

check.q: Who was the first woman to swim the English Channel?
check.why: Gertrude Ederle of New York crossed in 1926.

check.q: What is open water?

lessons.title: Olympic Races in the Sea
lessons.mainIdea: The first modern Olympic swimming races were held in the sea and a river; the first Olympic pool came in 1908.
reading: At the 1896 Olympics in Athens, swimmers raced in the cold sea near the port of Piraeus. Boats took them out, and they swam back to shore. Waves and wind changed every race.

At the 1900 Paris Games, swimmers raced in the Seine River. The current helped them go faster downstream. In 1904, in St. Louis, they swam in a lake at the fairgrounds. None of these times could be fairly compared.

In 1908, London built a 100-meter pool inside the main Olympic stadium. It was the first Olympic pool. That same year, swimming leaders met in London and formed *FINA*, the world swimming body. In 2022, FINA changed its name to *World Aquatics*.

words.d: the world swimming body, founded in London in 1908
the new name FINA took in 2022

lessons.title: Fifty Meters and Floating Ropes
lessons.mainIdea: Olympic pools became 50 meters long with lanes, while many American school pools are 25 yards.
reading: By the 1924 Olympics in Paris, swimming had a 50-meter pool. Floating ropes marked each swimmer's path. Olympic pools have been 50 meters ever since. This is called *long course*.

A *lane rope* is a line of floats stretched from wall to wall. It keeps swimmers apart. Newer ropes have spinning disks that calm the waves, so one swimmer's splash does not slow the next. World Aquatics rules set each lane at 2.5 meters wide.
Many American high school pools are 25 yards long. This is called *short course*. A 25-yard pool is shorter than a 25-meter pool. That is why record books always say which pool a time came from.

words.d: a 50-meter pool, the Olympic length
a 25-yard or 25-meter pool
a line of floats stretched across a pool to mark lanes and calm waves

lessons.title: A Touch Stops the Clock
lessons.mainIdea: A disputed finish in 1960 helped bring touchpads to swimming, and a 1972 race showed why times stop at hundredths.
reading: At the 1960 Olympics in Rome, John Devitt of Australia and Lance Larson of the United States finished the 100-meter freestyle almost together. Larson's hand timers showed a faster time. Yet the judges gave the gold medal to Devitt. People argued about it for years.
A *touchpad* solves that problem. It is a panel on the pool wall. When a swimmer touches it, the clock stops by itself. Touchpads were used at the Olympics starting in 1968, in Mexico City.

In 1972, in Munich, Gunnar Larsson of Sweden beat Tim McKee of the United States by two thousandths of a second. But pools are never built perfectly. A lane can be a few millimeters longer than the next. After that race, swimming times were kept to *hundredths* only.

words.d: a panel on a pool wall that stops the clock when a swimmer touches it
one second split into 100 equal parts

lessons.title: Who Could Get in the Water
lessons.mainIdea: Women first swam at the Olympics in 1912, and in Chicago in 1919 a boy died after crossing a racial line at a beach.
reading: Women's swimming races were added to the Olympics in 1912, in Stockholm. Fanny Durack of Australia won the 100-meter freestyle. Before that, many swimming clubs did not allow women to race at all.

In the early 1900s, many American beaches and pools were *segregated*. That means Black and white people were kept apart by law or by custom. In Chicago, the beach at 29th Street had an unmarked line in the water.

On July 27, 1919, a Black teenager named Eugene Williams floated on a raft past that line. White men threw rocks at him, and he drowned. Days of violence followed across Chicago. It became known as the Chicago *race riot* of 1919, and 38 people died.

words.d: separated by race, through laws or long-held customs

lessons.title: The Game of the Palm
lessons.mainIdea: Tennis began as jeu de paume, an indoor ball game in France and England, long before lawn tennis.
reading: In France in the 1100s and 1200s, people played a ball game called *jeu de paume*. The name means "game of the palm." At first, players hit the ball with their hands. Later they used rackets.

The game moved indoors into long stone halls with slanted roofs along the walls. Kings and nobles loved it. King Henry VIII of England played often. An old indoor court at Hampton Court Palace, near London, is still used today.
English speakers call that old game *real tennis* today. Where does the word "tennis" come from? One common explanation is the French word "tenez," meaning "take this." Historians are not fully sure.

words.d: "game of the palm"; an old French ball game that led to tennis
the English name today for the old indoor game played in walled halls

lessons.title: Wingfield's Box
lessons.mainIdea: Walter Wingfield introduced lawn tennis in 1873 and patented it in 1874, helped by new lawn mowers and rubber balls.
reading: Two inventions made a grass game possible. In 1830, Edwin Budding of England invented the *lawn mower*. Now lawns could be kept short and flat. In 1844, Charles Goodyear patented a way to make rubber strong and springy. Now balls could bounce on grass.

In 1873, a British army officer, Major Walter Clopton Wingfield, introduced a new outdoor game. In 1874 he took out a *patent* on it. A patent is a government paper that says an idea belongs to its inventor.

Wingfield sold his game in a box, with rackets, balls, a net and poles. He named it Sphairistike, from a Greek word for ball playing. His court was shaped like an hourglass, narrow at the net and wide at each end.

words.d: a government paper saying an invention belongs to the person who made it

lessons.title: Wimbledon Draws the Rectangle
lessons.mainIdea: In 1877, the first Wimbledon tournament used a rectangular court that became the model for courts everywhere.
reading: Wingfield's game spread fast, and players argued over rules. In 1875, the Marylebone Cricket Club in London published a set of lawn tennis rules. Clubs began to use one shared *rule book*.

In 1877, the All England Croquet and Lawn Tennis Club held a tournament at Wimbledon, near London. It used a *rectangle*, not an hourglass: 78 feet long and 27 feet wide. Twenty-two men entered. Spencer Gore won.

Today's singles court is still 78 feet by 27 feet. A doubles court is 36 feet wide. The net is 3 feet high in the center. The International Lawn Tennis Federation, formed in 1913, helped spread one court drawing around the world.

words.d: a tennis tournament near London, first held in 1877
a four-sided shape with four square corners
the written rules that everyone in a sport agrees to follow

lessons.title: Open Doors on the Court
lessons.mainIdea: Women's tennis championships began in the 1880s, and Black players, shut out of many clubs, built their own association in 1916.
reading: In 1881, the new United States National Lawn Tennis Association held its first national championship in Newport, Rhode Island. Richard Sears won. Wimbledon added a women's singles event in 1884, and Maud Watson won it.

For many years, most tennis clubs in the United States would not let Black players join. In 1916, Black players formed the *American Tennis Association*. It ran its own tournaments across the country.

Althea Gibson learned the game in New York and won many ATA titles. In 1950, she became the first Black player at the U.S. national championships. In 1956, she won the French Championships. In 1957, she won Wimbledon.

lessons.title: Tennis in Illinois Schools
lessons.mainIdea: Boys tennis became an IHSA state series early, with a first champion in 1912, the year before the world tennis federation formed.
reading: Tennis came to American schools soon after it reached American clubs. In Illinois, the IHSA crowned its first boys tennis champion in 1912. That was just twelve years after the association began.

A *state series* is a set of tournaments that ends in one state champion. For tennis, schools need courts built to one drawing. A court in Peoria must match a court in Chicago, or the matches would not be fair.

Like track, tennis was one of the earliest IHSA sports. Both depend on a shared measurement: a lap of known length, or a court of known size. That shared *standard* lets schools across the state play by one plan.
